claims.text: A hybrid framework coupling atomistic lattice-vibration simulations with NEGF electronic-transport calculations will separately predict lattice and electronic thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
Explicit inclusion of defects and minor oxygen impurities will make the conductivity predictions more accurate.
The hybrid method will reduce prediction error by approximately 30–40% relative to defect-free or Debye-temperature-dependent methods.
Experimentally produced HfNbTaTiZr samples contain realistic defect structures.
The modeled HfNbTaTiZr state contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Defects and oxygen impurities influence lattice dynamics in HfNbTaTiZr.
Defects and oxygen impurities influence electron scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Coupling between vibrational modes and electronic excitations is relevant to thermal transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Modeling atomistic vibrational modes and electronic excitations with defect- and impurity-induced scattering decouples lattice and electronic thermal-transport contributions.
Prior methods assumed perfect, defect-free crystals or relied on simplified parameters such as Debye temperature.
Prior approaches fail to capture impurity effects and realistic atomic-scale complexity.
Prior simplified analytical approaches conflate lattice and electronic transport.
Between 300 and 1200 K, the predicted total thermal conductivity will be 10–17 W/(K m) when lattice and electronic contributions are summed.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal conductivities will exhibit a crossover with comparable magnitudes.
The proposed method is applicable below 200 K and from 300 to 1200 K.
At intermediate or extreme temperatures, omitted quantum corrections or additional scattering mechanisms may limit the method.
The accuracy of the predicted improvement depends on the semi-empirical potentials and treatment of defect-induced scattering.
Integrating NEGF with atomistic dynamics for defective structures may reduce the precision with which lattice and electronic contributions can be separated.
